extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, labor economists, OFLC analysts, and stakeholders preparing comments or compliance materials on the Department of Labor's prevailing-wage/H-1B/LCA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates the Department of Labor's proposed standards, data practices, and legal/administrative criteria for setting prevailing wages and administering LCAs/H-1B/immigrant labor certification programs, intended for commenters and compliance practitioners. Useful for drafting regulatory comments, compliance checklists, or impact analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for prevailing wage determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing wage determinations are based on the wages of workers 'similarly employed' in the occupation and area of intended employment, as reflected in the OEWS survey (20 CFR 656.40(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the regulatory baseline for how prevailing wages should be set; agencies must rely on OEWS (Occupational Employment Wage Statistics) survey data to identify comparable wages for the occupation and geographic area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of wage level for position-specific requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The wage level may be adjusted based on the requirements of the position and the normal requirements for the occupation (DOL Prevailing Wage Determination Policy Guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning wage levels, agencies should consider the job's particular duties and qualifications; the policy guidance explains that position requirements can justify moving an assignment away from a default wage level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of O*NET to assess job complexity and inform wage level assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: O*NET provides detailed information on knowledge, skills, abilities, education, and work activities associated with occupations; in the context of prevailing wage determinations, O*NET is used to help assess the complexity and requirements of job duties, informing wage level assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOL uses O*NET to evaluate how education/experience/supervision map to wage levels; consider O*NET job zone and task descriptions when determining whether an occupation warrants a given wage level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for approximating wage-level percentiles (interpolation + optimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: To approximate wage levels, the Department combined Limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (L-BFGS) quasi-Newton optimization with linear interpolation to estimate percentile wage levels (I–IV) that align with a target average wage (Benchmark Value). The algorithm minimizes the difference between the mean wage predicted by assigned percentiles and the Benchmark Value using known percentiles (10, 25, 50, 75, 90) and linear interpolation to estimate the wage at a given percentile t (e.g., 35th percentile for Level I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the computational approach used to set wage-level cutoffs so that the weighted mean from chosen percentile cutoffs matches a benchmark; commenters should review assumptions, starting values, and interpolation choices when evaluating the methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of percentile cutoffs to ensure sufficiently differentiated wage levels
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department evaluated simulations (including starting values that would yield levels at the 45th, 56th, 66th, and 76th percentiles) and concluded such outcomes 'fail to sufficiently differentiate from one another to be useful.' The Department therefore chose percentile placements that produce greater differentiation across Levels I–IV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core criterion is that wage levels be meaningfully separated to permit granular employer wage assignments; methodology choices should be defensible on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate-level prevailing wage setting (reject occupation-specific approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department considered but rejected a more granular, occupation-specific approach to setting prevailing wages because such an approach would be unworkable; prevailing wages are set for all occupations and must reflect qualifications on an aggregate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy rationale: some high-volume LCA occupations include many jobs that do not require a bachelor's degree or 'highly specialized knowledge,' so aggregate-level wages are preferred to avoid using unsuitable comparison jobs as baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer attestation of non-adverse effect on U.S. workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers seeking to employ H-1B workers must attest on the Labor Condition Application (Form ETA-9035) that the employment of the foreign worker 'will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of workers in the United States similarly employed' (8 U.S.C. 1182(n)(1)(A)(ii); 20 CFR 655.731(a)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory/regulatory attestation is a mandatory element of LCAs and a legal touchstone for enforcement and compliance review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer documentation burden to substantiate LCA statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must 'develop sufficient documentation to meet its burden of proof with respect to the validity of the statements made in its LCA and the accuracy of information provided' (LCA Section J(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should compile contemporaneous records supporting job duties, recruitment, wages offered, and other LCA assertions; reviewers will expect documentation to substantiate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department authority to review and reject private surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations authorize the Department to review and reject private surveys that do not meet established criteria (see 20 CFR 656.40(b)(3) and 655.731(a)(2)(ii)(B)-(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private wage surveys used to establish prevailing wages must satisfy regulatory criteria; submissions relying on private surveys should demonstrate conformance with those standards to avoid rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data cleaning: removal of extreme wage outliers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed observations that reported wages smaller than $20,000 and larger than $500,000 from its analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing LCA or wage data, apply reasonable bounds to exclude implausible wage reports; the Department used these thresholds for dataset integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage normalization: convert all payment forms to annual pay using standard multipliers
rubrics_metrics.description: To create a single comparable wage variable, the Department converted all forms of payment into annual pay using standard period multipliers for both the offered wage and the prevailing wage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must normalize wages reported in hourly, weekly, monthly, or other periods to annual equivalents before comparison or aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'From' wage field as datapoint when 'To' absent
rubrics_metrics.description: The LCA wage field contains 'From' and 'To' entries for a wage range; because filling out the upper range is optional and only ~50% of LCAs have it, the Department used the number indicated in the 'From' field as the sole datapoint from F(a)(10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When wage ranges are partially reported, the Department defaults to the lower bound ('From') for analysis unless better data are available; commenters should note any bias this may introduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OEWS/OES vs. Survey data and rationale for dataset selection
rubrics_metrics.description: BLS produces public OES data in five wage levels, but the public data are not broken down with the level of granularity by area of employment needed to administer immigrant and nonimmigrant programs; consequently, the Department uses a separate dataset with two wage levels for program administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of data source matters for wage-level assignment; explain why a dataset's geographic or occupational granularity is or is not adequate for program use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of percent-difference metric between Survey and OES
rubrics_metrics.description: The '20% figure' represents the average percentage difference between Survey-based and OES prevailing wages across five key SOC codes in FY2024. For each SOC code, the Department calculated the mean prevailing wage for both Survey and OES sources, then computed the percentage difference relative to the OES baseline; the overall 20% is the mean of these five individual percentage differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting comparative gaps between data sources, disclose the SOCs used, the mean calculations, and the per-SOC percentage differences that compose the average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job Zone classifications inform occupational preparation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under O*NET, a 'job zone' groups occupations by the amount of education, experience, and on-the-job training required. Job Zone 4 includes occupations that require considerable preparation; Job Zone 5 includes occupations that require extensive preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Job zone assignments can be used to assess whether an occupation typically requires bachelor's-level education or extensive preparation relevant to the 'specialty occupation' inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard for 'specialty occupation' education/knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory references (e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b); 8 U.S.C. 1184(i)(1)(A)) describe the term 'specialty occupation' as requiring 'theoretical and practical application of a body of highly specialized knowledge' among other educational requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations that a position is a 'specialty occupation' must connect the job duties to a body of specialized knowledge consistent with statutory language and implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial standard: generalized bachelor's degree insufficient for 'specialty occupation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions (e.g., Chung Song Ja Corp. v. USCIS; Caremax Inc v. Holder) hold that permitting an occupation to qualify simply by requiring a generalized bachelor's degree would run contrary to congressional intent to provide a visa program for specialized, as opposed to merely educated, workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory or adjudicative findings should avoid characterizing occupations as 'specialty' solely because any bachelor's degree may be acceptable; must show field-specific specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations in matching historical BLS data to LCA year may understate wage gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: For analysis comparing BLS OEWS data to FY2020–2025 LCA data, the Department matched the BLS year to the corresponding year when the LCA was received; this 'effectively does not account for inflation' and leads to an overall underestimate of the gap between compensation received by immigrants/nonimmigrants and U.S. workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aligning survey-based prevailing wages with application filing dates, disclose potential temporal mismatches and inflationary effects that may bias estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: LCA filing can represent multiple putative employees (data deduplication caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: An LCA applicant can file an LCA on behalf of multiple putative H-1B employees; the Department used certain LCA fields as datapoints and acknowledges that many LCAs do not result in visas due to subsequent processing (e.g., lotteries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses that count LCAs as proxies for individual workers should account for multiple beneficiary filings and downstream attrition (lottery, denial), and commenters may supply data if distributions differ between cap-exempt and non-cap-exempt filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-discrimination norms regarding hiring of visa holders
rubrics_metrics.description: EEOC guidance notes that discrimination in favor of visa guest workers (and against U.S. workers) is illegal; examples include discriminatory job advertisements (such as 'H-1B preferred'), disparate treatment like differential benching/termination, and that common business reasons (customer preference, lower cost) do not excuse such discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory enforcement and employer compliance reviews should consider EEOC standards; attestations and recruitment practices must avoid discriminatory language or disparate treatment correlated with visa status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department may prioritize increasing Wage Level I to preserve differentiation if raising prevailing wages further
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Department sought to increase prevailing wage rates more than proposed, it would opt for an increase in the Wage Level I prevailing wage to preserve a sufficiently differentiated wage level system to permit employers to obtain more granular wage levels that reflect statutory factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy adjustments to prevailing-wage scales should consider how changes to one level affect the arithmetic setting of intermediate levels and maintain meaningful separation among levels.
